strengths: Well-motivated problem: Identifies genuine limitations in existing inference-time steering methods that overlook token-level causal influence
Principled methodology: Integrated Gradients choice is well-justified with clear explanation of theoretical properties (sensitivity, implementation invariance)
Comprehensive evaluation: Tests across both LLMs and VLMs, multiple safety-critical tasks, strong baselines, thorough ablations, and qualitative analysis
Consistent cross-model improvements: Demonstrates gains across diverse architectures (Llama, Qwen, LLaVA, Gemma) while preserving general capabilities
Practical efficiency: Reduces computational cost to ~96 seconds vs. 30-3600 minutes for LoRA fine-tuning
Reproducibility: Detailed experimental settings, hyperparameter analysis, GPU requirements, and full prompts in appendix
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Combines existing techniques (Integrated Gradients, PCA, activation steering) without substantial novel insight; contribution is primarily incremental
Modest improvements in many cases: FaithEval gains <1% for some models; MMHal-Bench improvements 1-5%, comparable to baselines; gains not always justify added complexity
No statistical significance testing: Single-run results without error bars or confidence intervals; unclear which improvements (ranging <1% to 13%) are statistically significant
Hyperparameter sensitivity: Non-trivial dependence on α, k, m with no principled selection method; requires development set tuning per task (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B peaks at α=6)
Limited direct validation of attribution: Relies solely on downstream task performance to validate attribution quality; no correlation with human annotations or ablations on identified tokens
Insufficient failure mode analysis: No discussion of when gradient-based attribution fails, effect of weak preference signals, or edge cases that challenge the method
Unexplored preference data sensitivity: No analysis of robustness to annotation noise or subjectivity; how does data quality affect steering?
Limited scope of steering objectives: Evaluation restricted to safety dimensions; no exploration of style, persona, factuality, or other steering goals
Weak theoretical justification: Why IG specifically? Why PCA aggregation? Method lacks formal analysis of convergence or optimality properties
Incomplete comparison with recent work: Acknowledges concurrent methods (Turner et al. 2024, Lin et al. 2025) but lacks detailed comparative analysis and differentiation
Generalization concerns: Only 2 LLM families at small-to-medium scales; unclear if findings scale to larger models or other families; multimodal applicability shown but not deeply explored
Missing code and accessibility: No mention of code release, limiting reproducibility and community adoption

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across both LLMs and VLMs on multiple safety/alignment benchmarks (TruthfulQA, Toxigen, FaithEval, MMHal-Bench, SPA-VL)
Clear problem motivation: identifies genuine limitations of existing steering methods that rely on fixed global interventions
Preservation of general model capabilities demonstrated (Tables 4-5 show BLEU, MMLU, MMMU scores remain competitive), addressing key concern about steering causing degradation
Sound technical approach combining theoretically grounded attribution (Integrated Gradients) with stable steering vector aggregation via PCA
Good ablation studies (Section 5.3) comparing attribution methods and modality-specific variants
Qualitative analysis with examples demonstrating behavioral improvements (Figures 4, 7)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core components are established techniques (IG from 2017, PCA standard practice, contrastive interventions from prior work); contribution is primarily engineering combination without new insights

Modest empirical improvements without statistical validation: TruthfulQA shows only +2.75 points vs. CAA, Toxigen +2.09 points, FaithEval +1.62 points; no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite small effect sizes

Critical methodological under-specification: preference pair generation not clearly explained for different datasets (how are dispreferred outputs created? annotated or model-generated?); this is central to the method but insufficiently detailed for reproducibility
Insufficient justification for design choices: why IG over modern alternatives (ablation only compares to 2017 SmoothGrad)? Why PCA? Why k=3-5? No principled guidance provided for practitioners
Small and arbitrary sample size for steering vector construction (50 samples); no analysis of stability or sensitivity to sample count
Incomplete failure analysis: no characterization of when/why method underperforms, missing discussion of failure modes despite modest improvements suggesting limited robustness

Computational cost claims lack rigor: 'negligible overhead' asserted without quantification of IG's multiple forward/backward passes; context for 502-second runtime missing; comparison to LoRA timing vague
No statistical significance testing despite 1-3 percentage point improvements that may be within noise
Limited theoretical insight into why this combination works; no mechanistic understanding beyond empirical results
Missing comparisons to some relevant baselines (RepE mentioned but not compared); recent mechanistic interpretability approaches not discussed

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B, LLaVA-1.6-7B, Qwen2.5-VL, Gemma-3.1-2B) and datasets with consistent improvements
Well-motivated problem: clearly articulates limitations of existing steering methods regarding token heterogeneity and multimodal challenges
Principled technical approach: principled use of Integrated Gradients over vanilla gradients with good justification (addresses saturation)
Thorough ablation studies validating design choices: token attribution methods, token count sensitivity, modality-specific variants, and objective functions
Demonstrates preservation of general capabilities (generation quality, reasoning) while steering behavior, crucial for practical deployment
Unified framework effective across both unimodal (LLMs) and multimodal (VLMs) settings—applicability across modalities is valuable
Clear presentation with good figures explaining the method and comprehensive appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines established techniques (Integrated Gradients, PCA, contrastive vectors) rather than introducing fundamentally new methods; main contribution is their application to multimodal steering

Computational overhead insufficiently analyzed: 96 seconds per steering objective stated but memory requirements and scalability to larger models (70B+) unclear; comparison to LoRA somewhat misleading as they solve different problems

Preference data dependency: method requires preference pairs for steering vector construction; Table 8 shows only modest gains of preference-based loss over standard likelihood; robustness to preference data quality unexplored
Modest LLM improvements (13.22% TruthfulQA, 7.08% Toxigen) raise questions about practical significance; VLM improvements more substantial but fewer qualitative examples
Experimental rigor concerns: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; small sample sizes (50 samples for steering construction); variance/stability not reported
Incomplete baseline comparisons: RepE mentioned as underperforming but without quantitative comparison; some recent steering methods lacking direct evaluation
Generalization questions unaddressed: cross-model transfer of steering vectors not analyzed; optimal token count k varies significantly across models without guidance for new architectures
Shallow failure analysis: limited discussion of failure modes; Section 5.2 provides only 2 qualitative examples; relationship between attribution scores and steering effectiveness not deeply explored

Attribution-steering connection underexamined: limited theoretical justification for why preference gradients identify causally influential tokens; robustness to conflicting preference signals not discussed

strengths: Strong and consistent empirical results across both LLMs and VLMs on safety-critical benchmarks (TruthfulQA +8.44-13.22%, MMHal-Bench hallucination reduction from 0.624 to 0.514, SPA-VL preference improvements 1-5%)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple baselines, extensive ablations, hyperparameter analysis, and cross-dataset generalization studies demonstrating the robustness of design choices

Well-motivated approach addressing a genuine limitation—existing methods apply global interventions without identifying which tokens drive undesirable behaviors; the three-stage pipeline is logically coherent
Valuable multimodal extension to VLMs with modality-aware analysis (Table 13) showing how attribution differs between visual and textual tokens
Demonstrates minimal degradation of general reasoning capabilities (MMLU drop of 3.64% vs. 17.8% for CAA), addressing a key concern with steering methods
Good experimental methodology with proper hyperparameter selection, clear implementation details, and evidence of reproducibility with promised code release
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—combines well-established components (Integrated Gradients from 2017, contrastive loss, PCA, layer-wise steering) without substantial innovation in individual techniques

Computational cost of vector construction insufficiently analyzed; while Table 7 shows minimal inference-time overhead, the cost of computing steering vectors via gradient estimation and PCA is not compared against alternatives like LoRA fine-tuning

Dependence on preference data quality not thoroughly investigated; no systematic study of how attribution and steering effectiveness vary with preference data size, diversity, or quality mismatches between training and test domains

Technical justification gaps: (1) Table 8 shows vanilla gradients are nearly as effective as IG (59.75% vs 59.75%), undermining the choice of IG; (2) normalization in Eq. 5 lacks theoretical or empirical justification; (3) IG baseline selection sensitivity unexplored

Scope limitations: evaluation heavily weighted toward safety/alignment tasks; improvements on general reasoning modest (MMLU 3.64% degradation); code generation, math, and other domains not evaluated; only 3 VLM models tested

Causality vs. attribution confusion—while IG identifies influential tokens, high attribution does not guarantee that intervening on these tokens will change behavior; the paper lacks formal causal validation beyond qualitative examples

Generalization concerns: cross-dataset transfer is sometimes marginal (e.g., RealToxicity generalization); unclear how vectors generalize across model sizes, fine-tuning histories, or out-of-distribution inputs; no failure mode analysis

Baseline comparison issues: some methods show competitive performance (CAA comparable on LLM tasks), no statistical significance testing reported, and VLM baseline comparisons are limited due to fewer available methods

Design choice justification: top-k token selection varies by model (k=3 for LLMs, k=20 for VLMs) without principled explanation; layer selection for steering injection lacks intuition; modest improvements of PCA over simpler alternatives (Table 9)

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple LLMs (Llama, Qwen) and VLMs (LLaVA, Gemma) with consistent improvements on safety-critical benchmarks (TruthfulQA, Toxigen, MMHal-Bench, SPA-VL)
Thorough ablation studies systematically analyzing hyperparameter sensitivity (λ, k), attribution methods, vector aggregation techniques, and layer-wise steering strategies
Practical inference-time applicability without retraining and minimal computational overhead (<5% throughput drop), making the method easy to deploy
Multimodal generality demonstrated across language-only and vision-language tasks, suggesting broad applicability
Good qualitative analysis with clear examples (Figures 4, 7, 8) showing the method correctly identifies and addresses problematic tokens
Extensive implementation details, experimental settings, and supplementary ablations supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: the method combines standard techniques (Integrated Gradients + contrastive activation steering) in a straightforward manner without clear differentiation from recent work (particularly CAA from Rimsky et al. 2024)
Modest empirical improvements over baselines, typically 1-3% absolute gains (e.g., TruthfulQA: 47.37 vs 44.62 for CAA), with no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported

Unclear and insufficient differentiation from CAA: the distinction is never explicitly stated in the main text; appears to be mainly 'CAA with token selection via IG' but this core difference is not clearly articulated

Methodological ad-hoc elements: the contrastive input construction strategy (masking/replacing tokens) lacks principled justification; the norm-preservation step (Eq. 5) is introduced late with minimal motivation despite apparent importance
Task-specific preference data requirement significantly limits generality and applicability; reduces practical deployment scope compared to general-purpose steering methods

Incomplete analysis of method behavior: limited insight into when/why the method works vs. fails; no systematic failure case analysis; insufficient exploration of design choice consequences (e.g., why attribution quality matters, what happens with poor preference data)
Modest and inconsistent improvements across modalities: helps hallucination reduction substantially but shows smaller gains on toxicity/reasoning tasks, without clear explanation of these differences

Experimental design gaps: no statistical significance testing; hyperparameter λ appears model-dependent; unclear if all baselines use equivalent experimental budgets (50 samples); limited to relatively small models (7-13B)
Cross-dataset generalization limited to single target dataset pair (Table 16), suggesting method may require task-specific steering vectors for new domains
Missing comparisons with other recent inference-time steering approaches and unclear positioning relative to the broader steering literature

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple LLM and VLM benchmarks with consistent, substantial improvements (8.44% on TruthfulQA, significant hallucination reduction on MMHal-Bench)
Unified multimodal approach that works effectively on both LLMs and VLMs without modality-specific engineering, demonstrating generality of the method
Thorough ablation studies validating all design choices: attribution methods, vector aggregation, hyperparameter sensitivity, layer-wise steering, and modality contributions
Well-motivated technical approach using integrated gradients over vanilla gradients with clear justification of advantages (sensitivity, implementation invariance)
Strong preservation of general model capabilities (MMLU, MMMU) showing steering doesn't degrade reasoning abilities
Computational efficiency with negligible overhead (~3.55% throughput drop) making it practical for deployment
Clear methodology presentation with good visualizations and comprehensive implementation details
Generalization analysis showing steering vectors transfer across datasets and tasks (Section 5.3)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines existing techniques (integrated gradients, contrastive attribution, layer-wise steering) rather than proposing fundamentally new methods
Lacks direct validation that identified 'influential' tokens are actually causing undesirable behaviors; this is inferred from steering results rather than verified independently
Dependence on preference data for training steering vectors; limited discussion of availability, quality, or definition of preferences for different task types
Hyperparameter selection challenges (k, λ) appear dataset/model-specific with no systematic guidance provided, requiring validation set resources
Incomplete comparisons with concurrent work; some recent steering methods mentioned but not experimentally compared
Limited analysis of failure modes and when/why the method fails; 'undercorrection' mentioned but not systematically studied
No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported, making it unclear which improvements are statistically reliable
Insufficient exploration of what patterns characterize influential tokens beyond modality information; limited mechanistic understanding
Brief limitations section without discussion of potential negative societal impacts or vulnerability to adversarial attacks
General capability preservation tested only on relatively straightforward tasks (MMLU, MMMU); more complex reasoning/generation tasks not evaluated
